mcqs.question: A query reads only one column from a table. Why does a row-oriented file layout still force it to touch every other column's bytes?
options: Because row-oriented files store each row's full set of columns contiguously, so reaching one column means reading past the others interleaved with it
Row-oriented files don't support single-column queries at all
This only happens if the table has no index
Row-oriented storage always duplicates every column value
mcqs.explanation: Because columns are interleaved within each row's contiguous block, there's no way to skip the other columns while reading one — you have to pass over them physically. Row layouts do support single-column queries, indexes are a separate concern from this physical layout issue, and nothing here involves duplicating values.

mcqs.question: A column has only 5 distinct values across a million rows. Which compression technique is best suited to it, and why?
options: Delta encoding, since it works best on columns with only a handful of distinct values
Dictionary encoding, since it stores each distinct value once and replaces occurrences with a small reference, shrinking a low-cardinality column dramatically
Run-length encoding, since it requires every value in the column to be identical
No compression technique applies to columns with repeated values
mcqs.explanation: Low cardinality is exactly what dictionary encoding exploits — a small number of distinct values means the dictionary stays tiny while every row shrinks to a small reference. Delta encoding targets increasing/slowly-changing numeric columns, not low-cardinality categories, and RLE needs long runs of the same value, not just a small set of distinct values scattered throughout.

mcqs.question: A row group's stored max value for order_date is 2024-05-15. A query filters WHERE order_date >= '2024-06-01'. What happens under predicate pushdown?
options: The engine reads the row group's data first, then discards non-matching rows afterward
The query fails because the filter doesn't match any stored value
Predicate pushdown only works on columns with dictionary encoding
The engine checks the row group's max stat, determines no row can match, and skips reading that row group's data entirely
mcqs.explanation: Predicate pushdown checks the cheap, pre-computed min/max stats before touching any actual data — if the max is provably below the filter's threshold, the whole row group is skipped with certainty. It doesn't require reading the data first, doesn't fail the query, and applies to numeric/comparable stats generally, not specifically dictionary-encoded columns.

mcqs.question: A table has 50 columns, and a query references 3 of them. What does column pruning do?
options: It reads all 50 columns then discards the unreferenced 47 after loading them into memory
It compresses the unreferenced columns instead of reading them
It reads only the 3 referenced columns' chunks from disk, never touching the other 47's bytes at all
It only works if the query also has a WHERE clause
mcqs.explanation: Because each column is a separate contiguous chunk, pruning simply never reads the bytes for unreferenced columns — it's a skip at the disk-read level, not a post-read filter. It doesn't load everything first, doesn't compress anything as part of pruning, and works independently of whether a WHERE clause is present.

mcqs.question: A 300-column table has columns that are queried by fewer than 1% of jobs. Why doesn't column pruning fully solve the cost problem this creates?
options: Column pruning doesn't work on tables with more than 100 columns
Storage cost still scales with all 300 stored columns, and any query using SELECT * still pays for all of them regardless of how rarely most are used
Rarely-used columns are automatically deleted by the storage engine
Pruning only reduces compute cost, never storage cost
mcqs.explanation: Pruning limits the damage for targeted queries, but the table's total storage footprint still reflects every stored column, and a SELECT * query still reads all 300 columns' bytes regardless of how rarely most are used elsewhere. Pruning has no column-count ceiling, unused columns aren't auto-deleted, and it primarily reduces bytes scanned per query, which affects both compute and scan cost.

mcqs.question: Why does late materialization avoid wasted work compared to reconstructing full rows before filtering?
options: It filters using isolated column scans first and only assembles full rows for the small set that survives, avoiding the cost of building rows that get discarded
It skips filtering entirely and returns all rows unfiltered
It only applies to queries with no WHERE clause
It reconstructs every row twice to double-check correctness
mcqs.explanation: By filtering against column chunks first and assembling full rows only for surviving positions, late materialization never pays the row-assembly cost for rows that end up discarded. It doesn't skip filtering or apply only to unfiltered queries, and it doesn't reconstruct rows twice — the whole point is doing that reconstruction as little as possible.
